# Introduction

In 1976, Bowles and Gintis argued that schooling reproduces economic inequality partly through the non-cognitive traits it cultivates and rewards [@bowles1976; @bowles2002schooling]. Family advantage can be transmitted through dispositions as well as money, qualifications and cognitive ability: children encounter different conditions for developing the behaviours valued in school and, later, in employment. Their correspondence argument placed the organisation of schooling and work at the centre of this process. The question behind today's interest in socio-emotional skills is therefore not new. It is whether characteristics that appear personal help convert unequal family circumstances into unequal educational outcomes.

Modern economics of skill formation gives this question a production interpretation. Families invest time and resources; schools supply instruction and learning environments; and existing capabilities affect what children gain from subsequent investment [@cunha2007]. Curiosity can encourage exploration, while perseverance can sustain effort. Advantaged families may have more opportunities to cultivate these dispositions and secure access to settings in which they support learning. This account differs from explaining rewards through conformity to workplace hierarchies, but it shares the concern that non-cognitive characteristics help transmit economic advantage. The present study examines the learning pathway, with school composition retained as part of the comparison.

This paper asks whether socio-emotional skills transmit socioeconomic advantage into reading achievement. It addresses three questions. Are these skills socially stratified? How much of the reading gradient runs through the combined skills pathway when school sorting is included? Which skills account for that pathway? Material deprivation provides a second exposure: among pupils with similar measured socioeconomic status, do unaffordable goods and activities connect to lower achievement through skills?

We use the student and school files from PISA 2025 and estimate each education system separately. The main comparison covers 69 systems that measure all six skills: perseverance, curiosity, enjoyment of problem solving, cognitive adaptability, goal setting and self-regulated help seeking. Together they contribute 437,776 pupils in 19,336 schools. The deprivation analysis covers 63 of these systems. A supplementary analysis retains systems with smaller observed skill blocks, rather than treating unmeasured skills as absent pathways.

The main result is a positive joint skills pathway in 53 of the 69 systems, with individual 95% intervals excluding zero; 48 retain support after correction for multiple testing. This is not a claim that the same mechanism has equal importance everywhere. In Denmark, a ten-percentile-point difference in family socioeconomic rank carries `r fmt(est('DNK','skills_sorting'))` reading points through skills. In Korea it carries `r fmt(est('KOR','skills_sorting'))` points, and in Malaysia `r fmt(est('MYS','skills_sorting'))`. Incorporating school sorting adds little to Denmark's estimate but substantially enlarges the pathway in Korea and Malaysia. Curiosity is the most widespread individual contributor. Korea illustrates why a common international skill ranking would nevertheless be misleading: its strongest positive contributions include enjoyment of problem solving and goal setting.

Previous cross-country studies already connect psychological characteristics to socioeconomic achievement gaps [@hofer2024; @gruijters2024; @avanesian2025]. This paper extends that evidence by separating a joint six-skill pathway within schools from the pathway incorporating the school composition associated with family circumstances. The counterfactual holds the socioeconomic profile fixed in the reading equation and replaces its joint skill profile with the one accompanying lower socioeconomic status. Keeping the school-average skill component in that replacement retains school allocation inside the account of transmission. A parallel deprivation analysis distinguishes relative socioeconomic position from the goods and activities a family cannot afford, at a given measured background. Both analyses report country-specific magnitudes and the individual skills contributing to them.

The development-policy question is whether support directed at pupils' skills leaves an appreciable pathway through school composition untreated. This distinguishes two margins for allocating scarce educational resources: helping disadvantaged pupils acquire and use skills, and improving the environments in which those pupils learn. The mediation estimates locate these margins; deciding between programmes also requires their costs, feasibility and effects. Keeping the full country set allows both weak and strong pathways to inform that decision.

Denmark, Korea and Malaysia are worked examples selected after estimation to explain contrasting combinations, not to represent their regions or rank policy performance. Denmark combines a positive skills pathway with an uncertain composition increment; Korea illustrates a larger composition component and a different skill mix; Malaysia adds evidence of a deprivation pathway to both features of the rank analysis. Germany and Mongolia provide counterexamples with uncertain joint rank pathways. All eligible systems remain in the figures and tables. These contrasts motivate country-specific investigation, rather than country groups chosen to maximise statistical significance.

# Previous evidence and research questions

## Investment, resource constraints and skill inequalities

The economics of skill formation treats skills as products of cumulative investment and as inputs into subsequent learning. Family resources influence the time, materials and experiences available to children; existing capabilities influence what children gain from later investment [@cunha2007]. Socio-emotional skills can enter this process through attention, persistence and engagement with difficult tasks. A pupil's capacity to organise study may therefore reflect past opportunities while also affecting the use of current educational inputs.

Economic research emphasises that these capabilities are multidimensional and that their measurement depends on behaviour and context [@almlund2011]. We use “socio-emotional skills” for six questionnaire scales: perseverance, curiosity, enjoyment of problem solving, cognitive adaptability, goal setting and self-regulated help seeking. Cognitive adaptability concerns adapting one's approach rather than performance on a cognitive test. Keeping the scales separate allows family advantage to have different relationships with each disposition.

OECD's social-and-emotional-skills framework translates the Big Five into five broad domains: task performance (conscientiousness), open-mindedness (openness to experience), engaging with others (extraversion), collaboration (agreeableness) and emotional regulation (emotional stability) [@kankaras2019]. Perseverance and curiosity map directly to the task-performance and open-mindedness families. The remaining PISA measures capture related problem engagement, adaptation and learning strategies. Their links to these domains are conceptual, not a claim that they are interchangeable Big Five scales. The six-index set therefore draws on OECD's Big Five-informed approach without constituting a complete inventory of all five domains.


Evidence from a randomized intervention in Colombia connects parental investments to improvements in early development [@attanasio2020]. At school age, teachers affect outcomes beyond test scores that predict later educational attainment [@jackson2018]. These findings give families and schools a role in producing capabilities, although neither establishes the size of adolescent skill inequalities in the present sample. Cross-country evidence is more directly relevant: @gruijters2024 find socioeconomic differences in the psychological characteristics measured in PISA 2018, alongside substantial variation in their contribution to achievement inequality.

The investment account suggests higher skill levels with greater socioeconomic resources, but relative position and immediate constraints need not capture the same process. Families with similar measured socioeconomic status can differ in their ability to afford clothes, leisure equipment or school participation. Such constraints may restrict exploration or make sustained engagement harder. We therefore examine both socioeconomic rank and material deprivation, separating differences among classmates from differences between school intakes.

> *RQ1. How are the six socio-emotional skills distributed by socioeconomic rank and material deprivation, within and between schools?*

## Skills as a transmission pathway, including school allocation

A socially stratified skill contributes to the achievement gradient only if it also enters the learning relationship. Two links are required: circumstances must predict skills, and those skill differences must predict achievement when the other skills are included. @hofer2024 document joint and separate mediation through five self-perceptions in the socioeconomic reading relationship across 70 PISA 2018 countries. Using a different set of measures and a decomposition of the socioeconomic science gap, @gruijters2024 find a modest contribution from the measured skills. Their contrast between advantaged and disadvantaged groups differs from the ten-rank-point reading contrast used here; the reported shares do not have interchangeable denominators. Together these studies motivate estimating the magnitude of transmission, rather than inferring it from a skill's correlation with achievement.

School allocation adds a further economic margin. Residential location, school choice and institutional rules affect the combination of peers, teaching and resources that pupils encounter. Evidence on school resources in Peru and on educational tracking across countries places these institutional differences within the explanation of achievement inequality [@leon2015; @hanushek2006]. The inheritance-of-inequality argument likewise identifies transmission routes beyond cognitive test performance [@bowles2002inheritance]. For this paper, the central issue is how the allocation of educational inputs changes the skills pathway into learning.

If advantaged pupils attend schools with higher average skills and stronger between-school skill--achievement relationships, a comparison confined to classmates can omit an important part of transmission. Compensatory school allocation can instead reduce that contribution. We compare the joint pathway holding school setting fixed with a pathway incorporating the school composition accompanying family circumstances. The same comparison for deprivation asks whether hardship carries an additional skills penalty at a given family and school socioeconomic status.

> *RQ2. How much of the reading gradient runs through the six skills jointly, and how does that pathway change when the school composition associated with socioeconomic rank or deprivation is included?*

## Which skills account for transmission?

The economic distinction is between capabilities that sustain investment in learning and those that influence how learning opportunities are used. Task-performance dispositions, including perseverance, can help pupils maintain effort when immediate rewards are small or tasks are difficult. Open-mindedness, including curiosity, can encourage information seeking and engagement with unfamiliar ideas. In a skill-production account, both matter: time spent studying and the learning gained from that time need not be governed by the same disposition [@cunha2007; @almlund2011]. This gives substantive reasons to examine different skills separately, rather than treat any desirable trait as an equivalent educational input.

@avanesian2025 provide relevant evidence using OECD SSES data on 44,394 pupils aged 10 and 15 in eight cities. Their mixed-effects models relate five broad skill domains to a grade-based high-achievement indicator. Task performance and open-mindedness are the strongest positive predictors; the relationships for other domains are less uniform, including a nonlinear collaboration pattern. Their comparison of SES groups also shows why similar skill levels need not eliminate an achievement gap: the high-SES advantage persists, and the plotted task-performance and open-mindedness slopes are largely parallel. These results motivate distinguishing the contribution of particular skills from a general claim that more non-cognitive skill necessarily equalises achievement.

The present analysis moves from broad domains to six specific PISA indices and from high grades to reading proficiency. Curiosity and perseverance provide the clearest links to the two domains highlighted by Avanesian and Rozhkova. Enjoyment of problem solving captures engagement with demanding tasks; goal setting captures study management; help seeking depends on recognising difficulty and obtaining support. Their reading relationships may differ because instructional demands and access to useful assistance differ. This is a reason to investigate country and school-level patterns, not to infer institutional causes from country labels.

A skill's contribution also requires a socioeconomic gradient in its distribution. A strong reading predictor carries little advantage if it is evenly distributed; a strongly stratified skill contributes little when its reading relationship is weak after other skills enter. Earlier decomposition work distinguishes such differences in endowments from differences in returns [@gruijters2024]. Material deprivation may shift the balance: restricted participation can constrain exploration, while insecure resources can make sustained engagement harder. We therefore compare the joint-model contributions across skills, exposures and systems without imposing a universal ranking or assuming every contribution is positive.

> *RQ3. Which socio-emotional skills contribute to the socioeconomic and deprivation pathways, and how does their composition differ across education systems?*

# Data and empirical strategy

## Sample, outcome and exposures

The analysis uses the PISA 2025 public-use student and school files and accompanying questionnaire documentation [@oecd2026data]. The source snapshot contains 90 systems and 755,721 pupils. A system may be a country or a participating subnational population. We use the documented sample labels, rather than interpreting every estimate as nationally representative. Model eligibility requires valid reading values, socioeconomic status, an observed skill block, school identifiers and survey weights, together with at least 100 complete pupils and 30 schools.

SES models can be estimated in 82 systems. The main analysis uses the 69 with all six skills, selected on measurement coverage. The remaining 13 appear in the supplement, with their observed skill counts. Deprivation models are available in 75 systems overall and 63 of the full-six-skill systems. The main samples contain 437,776 and 397,940 pupils, respectively. Table 1 describes the analytical coverage; the supplement lists every system, exclusions and descriptive statistics. We use reading throughout and do not substitute another achievement domain where reading is unavailable. Complete-case coverage is especially low in Armenia (21.6%) and Lebanon (30.1%). A descriptive audit attributes the sequential losses to missing SES and incomplete skill indices, rather than unavailable reading values or school weights. Retained pupils score about 40 and 52 reading points higher, respectively, than excluded pupils with observed reading. These two estimates describe selected complete cases; their intervals do not restore national representativeness. The supplement reports the exclusion sequence and comparisons.

```{r}
#| results: asis
cov <- A[status=='Eligible',.(Systems=.N,Students=sum(N),Schools=sum(schools)),by=.(Exposure=exposure,Block=ifelse(skills==6,'Six skills','Fewer skills'))]
cov<-cov[order(match(Exposure,c('SES','DEP')),match(Block,c('Six skills','Fewer skills')))]
cov[,Exposure:=ifelse(Exposure=='SES','Socioeconomic rank','Material deprivation')]
cov[,Students:=num(Students)];cov[,Schools:=num(Schools)]
tbl(cov,'Analytical coverage. Each system is estimated separately; students and schools are unweighted sample counts.',size=9)
```

Reading achievement is represented by ten plausible values, each analysed separately before combining estimates and uncertainty. Family SES is the PISA index of economic, social and cultural status (ESCS). We convert ESCS into a survey-weighted midpoint percentile rank within each system, using all pupils with valid ESCS and final student weights before complete-case selection. Dividing this rank by ten makes a unit a ten-percentile-point difference on the national socioeconomic ladder. It is neither an income percentage nor a common absolute resource difference across countries.

The six skill indices are the OECD's released weighted-likelihood scores, not averages constructed for this study. The supplement maps each to its questionnaire block and item identifiers [@oecd2025questionnaire; @oecd2025codebook]. Two labels require care: goal setting includes planning, checking understanding and changing study strategy; self-regulation focuses on help seeking. Cognitive adaptability includes responses to unfamiliar situations and interpersonal difficulties. These are related learning dispositions and behaviours, rather than six interchangeable personality traits.

Each released index is standardized using its weighted mean and standard deviation in the country's SES analytic sample; the deprivation sample retains that transformation. A coefficient is therefore per country-specific pupil skill SD, including when a school mean appears in the equation. We neither impute missing skill indices nor require every underlying item to be answered when OECD supplies a score. The main models require all six released indices. Growth mindset is excluded because a belief about the malleability of ability is conceptually distinct from the six measures retained here.


Deprivation counts items reported as unavailable because the family cannot afford them. “Yes” and “No, other reason” both contribute zero. Nine items are candidates. The four core possessions are properly fitting shoes, new clothes, outdoor leisure equipment and indoor games; five further items cover activities or participation. Within each system, an item is retained when at least 90% of respondents answering any candidate item provide a valid response to it. This operational rule identifies the observed item set; pupils missing any retained item are excluded from that exposure model. An absent module is treated as missing, not as no deprivation. The 63 main systems use three to nine items in 13 distinct combinations. A common-four-item sensitivity analysis separates the consequences of item selection from sample composition.

## Regressions for the two links

For pupil $i$ in school $j$, let $X_{ij}$ denote rank divided by ten, or the deprivation count. Define the weighted school mean $\bar X_j$, and $X^W_{ij}=X_{ij}-\bar X_j$. We make the same decomposition for every skill and control. Thus status is demeaned within schools, while its school mean remains explicitly in the model. This retains the between-school dimension relevant to inequality. The method follows the correlated-effects logic of including group means [@mundlak1978], with a random intercept for each school and fixed slopes within each system.

The **skill equation (M1)** is fitted separately for each skill $k$:

$$
M_{kij}=\alpha_k+a_{Wk}X^W_{ij}+a_{Bk}\bar X_j+
\gamma_{Wk}'C^W_{ij}+\gamma_{Bk}'\bar C_j+u_{kj}+e_{kij}.
$$ {#eq-m1}

Here $a_W$ is the within-school exposure-to-skill gradient, and $a_B$ the corresponding gradient between school means. The **achievement equation (M2)** includes all six skills jointly:

$$
\begin{split}
Y_{ij}={}&\alpha+c'_WX^W_{ij}+c'_B\bar X_j+
\sum_{k=1}^{6}\{b_{Wk}M^W_{kij}+b_{Bk}\bar M_{kj}\}\\
&+\beta_W'C^W_{ij}+\beta_B'\bar C_j+v_j+\epsilon_{ij}.
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-m2}

The $b$ coefficients are the second link: reading points per skill standard deviation, at the relevant level, with the other skills included. The $c'$ coefficients describe the exposure gradient remaining after skills enter. A baseline achievement model (M0) omits the skill terms and supplies the pre-skill reading gradients. It is not the denominator of the mediated share reported below.

Controls are the recorded non-male gender indicator and age centred at 15, each entered as a within-school deviation and a school mean. Age is unavailable in Norway, which is in the supplementary partial-block sample. Every deprivation equation additionally includes raw ESCS and its school mean. All equations for an exposure use the same complete-case sample, and school means are recalculated for that sample.

Including school means addresses the part of non-random allocation reflected in observed composition. It also prevents a single SES coefficient from mixing the family comparison within schools with the comparison across schools. We then measure the observed association between the two through a final-student-weighted **sorting projection (S)**:

$$
\bar X_j=\eta+\delta X_{ij}+\pi'C_{ij}+\omega'\bar C_j+r_{ij}.
$$ {#eq-sort}

The coefficient $\delta$ calibrates how much school-average exposure differs with a one-unit difference in individual exposure, holding the controls fixed. This is an auxiliary projection, not another random-intercept achievement regression. Table 2 maps each question to its estimation step.

```{r}
#| results: asis
x <- data.table(Question=c('RQ1: Are skills stratified?','RQ2: How much runs through skills?','RQ2: What does school composition add?','RQ3: Which skills carry it?'),
 Model=c('M1: one mixed model per skill','M1 + M2: joint mediation','M1 + M2 + S','Skill terms from M1 + M2 + S'),
 Quantity=c('$a_W$, $a_B$: skill SD per exposure unit','$I_W$, $I_S$: reading points through all skills','$\\Delta_S=I_S-I_W$: added skills pathway','$I_{S,k}$: reading points assigned to skill $k$'))
tbl(x,'Research questions, models and reported quantities. Each row applies to socioeconomic rank and material deprivation. M2 contains all six skills; S supplies the sorting coefficient used in $I_S$.',size=8,widths=c('3.4cm','4.5cm','6.4cm'),long=FALSE,escape=FALSE)
```

## Joint multilevel mediation

The within-school joint pathway is $I_W=\sum_k a_{Wk}b_{Wk}$. The between-school pathway, per unit of school-average exposure, is $I_B=\sum_k a_{Bk}b_{Bk}$. They concern different comparisons and cannot simply be added [@preacher2010]. For an individual exposure difference of one unit, the sorting projection supplies a school-mean difference of $\delta$ and a within-school difference of $1-\delta$. The resulting joint contrast is

$$
I_S=(1-\delta)I_W+\delta I_B,\qquad
\Delta_S=I_S-I_W=\delta(I_B-I_W).
$$ {#eq-joint}

The counterfactual question is: **how much lower would predicted reading be at the higher socioeconomic profile if its skills instead followed the profile associated with lower socioeconomic status?** The two profiles differ by ten national rank points. In the reading equation, we hold the higher profile's own and school-average socioeconomic status, individual and school-average controls, and fitted response coefficients fixed. We replace the six skills jointly, including both their within-school deviations and their school means. The difference between these two reading predictions is $I_S$.

The replacement has two parts. The lower profile carries a different skill position among classmates and a different school-average skill profile. Their fitted mean differences are $(1-\delta)a_{Wk}$ and $\delta a_{Bk}$ for skill $k$. Holding the school component fixed gives $I_W$; retaining the composition associated with family circumstances gives $I_S$. These are comparisons between profiles on the baseline national rank scale. They do not require every pupil to move up that scale simultaneously.

For deprivation, the higher exposure profile has one more unaffordable item, with family and school ESCS held fixed. We compare its predicted reading under the skill profile accompanying greater hardship with its prediction under the skill profile accompanying one fewer item. A negative $I_S$ is therefore a reading penalty through skills. In both analyses, only the skill inputs change between the two outcome predictions.

This is a joint distributional mediation calculation in an additive multilevel model. The mediator vector contains six within-school deviations and six school means. Only their fitted means enter the additive reading prediction; a unique full joint distribution is not required. Integrating over any joint skill distributions with those means gives exactly the products in @eq-joint. The products are therefore a way to compute the chosen contrast, rather than a substitute for defining mediation. The approach draws on counterfactual mediation and joint interventional contrasts [@imai2010; @vansteelandt2017]. It neither requires independent skill residuals for this additive mean contrast nor estimates an ordered chain among the six skills. We calculate it directly from the mixed models; we do not fit six separate single-mediator models with the `mediation` package.

Each skill contributes $I_{S,k}=(1-\delta)a_{Wk}b_{Wk}+\delta a_{Bk}b_{Bk}$. These terms sum to $I_S$. The remaining component is $D=(1-\delta)c'_W+\delta c'_B$, and the coherent model-implied total is $T=D+I_S$. The mediated percentage is $100I_S/T$, calculated for each plausible value and then combined. We report it only when the total has a stable sign and the components support a proportional interpretation. Reading-point contrasts remain available when that condition fails. The original sign and component screen admits 68 of 69 SES shares and 40 of 63 deprivation shares. For display, we additionally withhold percentages whose 95% intervals extend below zero and above 100%; this removes five deprivation shares, leaving 35. Their reading-point decompositions remain available. This conservative precision rule changes presentation, not the estimated pathways.

## Computation and uncertainty

All models are estimated in R 4.4.1. The main estimator uses the Gaussian two-level survey-weighted likelihood implemented by WeMix, with an optimized calculation from school-level sufficient statistics for the repeated bootstrap fits [@wemix; @rabe2006]. Conditional student weights are obtained by dividing final student weights by school weights and scaling them to the analytic pupil count within each school. School weights enter at the school level. The fitted regression specification is a random-intercept within--between model, not a random-slope model. The supplement provides the exact R formulas and validation results.

Unweighted `lme4::lmer()` fits of the same formulas provide a sensitivity comparison [@bates2015]. We retain WeMix because `lmer()`'s weight argument concerns residual precision and does not implement the two survey-weight levels required here. In particular, changing the estimator should not silently change what the weights mean.

Uncertainty is computed from 499 whole-school bootstrap draws per country and exposure. Each draw re-estimates the skill equations, reading equations and sorting projection, and recalculates the joint pathway. For ten reading plausible values, total variance is the mean bootstrap variance plus 1.1 times the variance of the ten point estimates. We show normal-approximation 95% intervals. Secondary tables retain Benjamini--Hochberg adjustments from the full estimable-system analysis, separately by exposure and test family [@benjamini1995]. Counts of directional evidence supplement country estimates; they are not estimates of an international average or tests of differences between countries.

# Results

## Social gradients are widespread, but do not establish transmission by themselves

The first link is evident across much of the main sample. Within-school SES gradients are positive with intervals excluding zero in `r supported('aW_CURIO')` systems for curiosity, `r supported('aW_PERSEV')` for perseverance, `r supported('aW_ENPROBS')` for enjoyment of problem solving, `r supported('aW_COGABIL')` for cognitive adaptability, `r supported('aW_GOALSET')` for goal setting and `r supported('aW_SELFREG')` for self-regulated help seeking. The corresponding between-school counts are `r supported('aB_CURIO')`, `r supported('aB_PERSEV')`, `r supported('aB_ENPROBS')`, `r supported('aB_COGABIL')`, `r supported('aB_GOALSET')` and `r supported('aB_SELFREG')`. The complete country coefficients and intervals are indexed in the supplement and supplied in `tables/country_link_coefficients.csv`: prefixes `aW_` and `aB_` identify the within- and between-school skill gradients, and `bW_` and `bB_` identify the reading relationships. The file includes every estimable system and both exposures.

The gradients differ in magnitude across systems. In Denmark, ten SES rank points correspond to `r ci('DNK','aW_CURIO',digits=3)` standard deviations of curiosity within schools. Malaysia's estimate is `r ci('MYS','aW_CURIO',digits=3)`, and Korea's is `r ci('KOR','aW_CURIO',digits=3)`. The differences per ten rank points are modest fractions of a skill standard deviation, but that is a scale statement, not evidence that the socioeconomic gradient is absent or irrelevant to learning.

The second link distinguishes stratification from transmission. Denmark's within-school curiosity coefficient in the reading equation is `r ci('DNK','bW_CURIO')` points per skill standard deviation. Korea's is `r ci('KOR','bW_CURIO')`. A positive social gradient in curiosity therefore does not imply the same reading pathway in these two systems. This is why the joint mediation estimates, rather than the social gradients alone, answer the central question.

@fig-gap-link makes the two links visible for every system. Moving right means a larger socioeconomic skill difference among classmates; moving up means a stronger skill--reading relationship after including the other five skills. Their product is the within-school contribution of that skill. The dashed curves mark equal contributions, so a larger skill gap can offset a weaker reading relationship. This is a decomposition of the fitted pathway, not a cross-country regression. The companion figure in the supplement displays the between-school links; the joint contrast below combines both levels with the observed school composition.

![Socioeconomic skill gaps and their reading relationships within schools. Each panel uses saved M1 and M2 point estimates for all 69 six-skill systems. Dashed curves mark products of 0.25, 0.5 and 1 reading point per ten rank points, from lower to higher curves. The three labelled systems are the worked examples in the text.](../04_output/rev1/figures/ses_gap_link_w.pdf){#fig-gap-link width=100% fig-pos='H'}

## The combined skills pathway carries advantage in most systems

@fig-ses displays all 69 country estimates, with and without the school component. The pathway allowing for sorting is positive with a 95% interval excluding zero in 53 systems and uncertain in 16; none has a negative interval excluding zero. After adjustment for multiple testing, 48 retain support. The result is broad evidence for a skills route, alongside meaningful variation in its magnitude and precision.

The worked examples make the unit interpretable. Denmark's pathway is `r ci('DNK','skills_sorting')` reading points per ten rank points, accounting for `r fmt(est('DNK','share'),1)`% of its model-implied total gradient. Malaysia's pathway is `r ci('MYS','skills_sorting')` points and `r fmt(est('MYS','share'),1)`%. Korea's is `r ci('KOR','skills_sorting')` points and `r fmt(est('KOR','share'),1)`%. For Malaysia, the `r fmt(est('MYS','skills_sorting'))`-point contrast means that predicted reading at the higher socioeconomic profile falls by that amount when its joint skill profile is replaced by the one accompanying a profile ten rank points lower, with the other inputs held fixed. These percentages concern different national gradients. They do not imply that Korea has the largest overall SES gap or that its schools generate the largest causal return to a skills programme.

Germany provides a useful counterpoint: its combined pathway is `r ci('DEU','skills_sorting')` points. Mongolia's is `r ci('MNG','skills_sorting')`. Both intervals include zero. A small or uncertain net pathway can arise from weak links or from offsetting skill contributions; it does not require every skill to be unrelated to achievement. We retain these estimates alongside the positive cases.

## Which skills carry the pathway?

Curiosity is the most widespread positive contributor: its individual pathway is positive with an interval excluding zero in 48 systems, compared with 24 for perseverance. The corresponding counts are eight for cognitive adaptability, seven each for enjoyment of problem solving and self-regulated help seeking, and four for goal setting. These counts concern contributions after all six skills enter together, rather than separate regressions giving each skill credit for shared variation.

@fig-ses-skills shows the complete country pattern. Curiosity contributes `r ci('DNK','indS_CURIO')` reading points in Denmark and `r ci('MYS','indS_CURIO')` in Malaysia. Korea is different. Its curiosity contribution is `r ci('KOR','indS_CURIO')`, while enjoyment of problem solving contributes `r ci('KOR','indS_ENPROBS')` and goal setting `r ci('KOR','indS_GOALSET')`. The combined Korean pathway is strong even though curiosity does not carry it clearly.

Goal setting illustrates another distinction. Its within-school social gradient is positive in 64 systems, yet its joint contribution to reading is positive in only four and negative in ten, with the remaining intervals including zero. The data therefore do not support treating a socially advantaged disposition as automatically productive for reading, conditional on the other skills. The pattern is compatible with differences in what the scale measures in practice, overlaps among dispositions, and the uses to which pupils put them. It does not imply that setting goals generally damages learning.

![Skill-specific contributions to the socioeconomic pathway in every full-six-skill system. Colours show reading points, with zero at the centre. White dots indicate individual 95% intervals excluding zero. Each cell is part of the same joint model; cells sum across skills to the country pathway in @fig-ses.](../04_output/rev1/figures/ses_skills.pdf){#fig-ses-skills width=100% fig-pos='H'}

## School sorting changes how much advantage runs through skills

The sorting comparison matters most where the between-school skill pathway exceeds the within-school one and family rank is related to school rank. The addition $\Delta_S$ is positive with an interval excluding zero in 27 of the 69 systems, with 23 retaining support after adjustment. In 42 systems the addition is uncertain. No system has a negative addition established by its individual interval.

Korea's pathway rises from `r ci('KOR','skills_same_school')` points with school setting fixed to `r ci('KOR','skills_sorting')` when sorting is included. The addition itself is `r ci('KOR','sorting_increment')` points. Malaysia's corresponding addition is `r ci('MYS','sorting_increment')`. These are intervals for the difference, recalculated within each bootstrap draw; the conclusion does not come from comparing the significance of two separate estimates.

Denmark shows why sorting should be estimated rather than assumed to amplify the route. Its fixed-setting pathway is `r ci('DNK','skills_same_school')` and its sorting addition is `r ci('DNK','sorting_increment')`. The joint pathway is positive, but the school extension adds little. Differences among classmates account for most of the estimated skill route in that comparison.

The economic implication is that a student-level account can miss an appreciable part of skill-mediated inequality in some systems. It does not follow that all school socioeconomic differences operate through the measured skills. The remaining component continues to contain other connections between resources, schools and reading. Nor is a positive sorting addition the effect of moving a pupil to a different school: it is the contribution of the observed school component to the specified profile contrast.

## Material deprivation carries a skills penalty in a smaller set of systems

The deprivation results address hardship after accounting for both family and school ESCS. The joint pathway is negative with an interval excluding zero in 25 of the 63 systems, positive in none and uncertain in 38. Eighteen retain support after multiple-testing adjustment. The sorting addition is negative in nine systems by the individual interval criterion, with four retaining adjusted support. @fig-dep retains the positive and imprecise point estimates as well as the negative results.

Malaysia's deprivation pathway is `r ci('MYS','skills_sorting','DEP')` reading points per additional unaffordable item. Its model-implied total is `r ci('MYS','total','DEP')`, of which the skills route accounts for `r fmt(est('MYS','share','DEP'),1)`%. The result asks whether hardship matters among pupils with similar measured background, not whether ESCS has ceased to matter. Curiosity carries `r ci('MYS','indS_CURIO','DEP')` points of this penalty.

Mongolia and the Philippines also show negative joint pathways: `r ci('MNG','skills_sorting','DEP')` and `r ci('PHL','skills_sorting','DEP')` points, respectively. Their exposure definitions differ: Mongolia retains four items, while the Philippines and Malaysia retain six. A one-item difference does not necessarily represent the same severity or type of deprivation. Denmark's and Korea's joint deprivation intervals include zero. In Korea, the model-implied total also has an unstable sign, so a mediated percentage would be misleading and is withheld.

\clearpage

![Country-specific joint deprivation pathways in the 63 full-six-skill systems. Negative values indicate a reading penalty transmitted through skills per additional unaffordable item, accounting for individual and school ESCS. Brackets after system names give the retained item count; equal counts can still represent different item sets. Bars are individual 95% bootstrap/PV intervals.](../04_output/rev1/figures/dep_pathways.pdf){#fig-dep width=100% fig-pos='H'}

\clearpage

The skill composition also differs from the rank analysis. Curiosity and perseverance each carry negative contributions in 15 systems by the individual interval criterion; self-regulated help seeking does so in five, cognitive adaptability in four, goal setting in two and enjoyment of problem solving in one. Adjusted support is less widespread: eight for curiosity, three for perseverance and two for self-regulated help seeking. @fig-dep-skills shows the country estimates without forcing a common hardship mechanism onto every system.

The first link is informative here. Greater deprivation predicts lower perseverance within schools in 38 systems, compared with 16 for curiosity. Yet both skills have negative joint reading contributions in 15 systems. Hardship can thus have a widespread gradient in a disposition without that disposition explaining the reading penalty everywhere. This reinforces the value of estimating the two links together.

![Skill-specific contributions to the deprivation pathway. Values are reading points per additional unaffordable item, including the school sorting component. White dots mark individual 95% intervals excluding zero. The scale differs from @fig-ses-skills because the exposure and magnitude differ.](../04_output/rev1/figures/dep_skills.pdf){#fig-dep-skills width=100% fig-pos='H'}

## Evidence across the research questions and sensitivity checks

Table 3 summarises the country evidence. “Support” means the interval excludes zero in the direction suggested by the resource argument: positive for rank, negative for deprivation. “Opposite” uses the reverse direction; “uncertain” means the interval includes zero. The joint pathway and sorting rows address RQ2; skill-specific rows address RQ3. They describe the prevalence of each pattern, without requiring every skill to transmit advantage. RQ1 counts appear in the supplement. The country estimates remain the primary results.

```{r}
#| results: asis
s <- rbind(cbind(Exposure='SES',summary_h()),cbind(Exposure='Deprivation',summary_h('DEP')))
s[,Systems:=NULL]
tbl(s,'Country evidence for the joint pathway, sorting addition and skill contributions. Denominators: 69 SES systems and 63 deprivation systems. BH support uses the retained full-analysis testing families.',size=7.6,widths=c('1.8cm','4.6cm',NA,NA,NA,NA))
```

Several checks clarify the scope of these findings. Unscaled conditional weights preserve the direction of the joint estimate in 68 of 69 main SES systems and all 63 deprivation systems. Restricting to schools with at least ten analytic pupils preserves it in 68 and 57 systems, respectively. These are point-estimate comparisons, not new interval-based tests. The common-four deprivation definition is available in 61 main systems and preserves the direction in 55. In Malaysia it changes the joint estimate from `r fmt(est('MYS','skills_sorting','DEP'))` to `r fmt(V[CNT=='MYS' & variant=='core_four_same_sample' & term=='skills_sorting',estimate])` points per item on the same pupils.

Magnitude sensitivity is not uniform. Among the 69 main SES systems, the largest absolute change under weight rescaling is 0.51 reading points in the Philippines. Restricting to schools with at least ten analytic pupils changes Lebanon's pathway by 1.55 points, against its low complete-case coverage. Unweighted estimation changes Thailand's pathway by 1.75 points. For deprivation, the largest changes are 1.62 points under weight rescaling in Croatia, 2.63 under the school-size restriction in Belgium, 2.10 under unweighted estimation in the United Kingdom, and 3.97 under the common-four-item definition in Serbia. The last changes the exposure itself. None of these saved point comparisons supplies a new confidence interval or independently establishes a changed mechanism.

Weighting can matter substantively. Malaysia's unweighted `lmer()` SES pathway is `r fmt(L[CNT=='MYS' & exposure=='SES' & term=='skills_sorting',lmer_unweighted])` points, compared with the weighted `r fmt(est('MYS','skills_sorting'))`; Korea's is `r fmt(L[CNT=='KOR' & exposure=='SES' & term=='skills_sorting',lmer_unweighted])`, compared with `r fmt(est('KOR','skills_sorting'))`. These comparisons support retaining a survey-weighted main specification, rather than treating the estimator choice as inconsequential. The supplement reports all countries, omitted-variable stress tests and the systems with incomplete skill blocks. The latter broaden coverage but do not estimate an unobserved six-skill pathway.

@fig-robustness compares magnitudes directly. A country on the diagonal has the same joint pathway in the main and alternative specifications; departures show how much it changes. Each panel uses the same scale, and the three largest absolute changes are labelled. The supplement provides the equivalent deprivation comparison, including the common-four-item definition. These displays complement the direction counts by showing whether a similar sign conceals a substantial change in the estimated pathway.

![Sensitivity of the joint socioeconomic skills pathway to weight scaling, minimum school sample size and the unweighted mixed-model estimator. Each panel retains all 69 six-skill systems. The diagonal denotes identical estimates. These are saved point-estimate comparisons; the alternatives have no new bootstrap intervals.](../04_output/rev1/figures/ses_robustness.pdf){#fig-robustness width=100% fig-pos='H'}

# Discussion

## From non-cognitive traits to the production of learning

The positive skills pathway in 53 systems gives renewed empirical relevance to an older economic question: how do family circumstances become personal characteristics that carry advantage? @bowles1976 placed non-cognitive traits and the organisation of schooling within an account of economic reproduction. Bowles, Gintis and Osborne subsequently argued that differences in behaviour and preferences help explain economic success beyond schooling and measured cognitive ability [@bowles2001behavioral]. These arguments make the distribution of dispositions part of the explanation of inequality, rather than an alternative to it.

Their behavioural account also distinguishes productive capacities from preferences that make effort easier to elicit. Employers can reward the latter even when they are not skills in the conventional production-function sense [@bowles2001incentive]. This distinction matters for interpreting our findings. Curiosity's widespread contribution to reading points towards engagement with learning; perseverance suggests sustained effort. Neither is evidence that schools reward conformity to workplace hierarchy. The contribution of this study is to locate a skills pathway into demonstrated reading proficiency, an educational stage at which socioeconomic advantage can accumulate before labour-market entry.

The skill-formation framework of @cunha2007 supplies the more direct interpretation. Earlier capabilities and investments shape what children gain from subsequent learning opportunities. Our two links fit that sequence: family position predicts the distribution of skills, and those differences enter the reading gradient. The counterfactual gives the economic content of the decomposition: it removes the skill endowment difference while retaining the higher socioeconomic profile in the reading equation. The remaining component captures the advantage transmitted through inputs outside the measured skill block. Because the fitted skill coefficients do not vary with SES, the comparison concerns differences in skill endowments at a common response within each level, rather than socioeconomic differences in returns to the same skill. Curiosity can therefore reflect both accumulated opportunities for exploration and a capability used in further learning. The result is consistent with cumulative investment; the dynamic process itself remains a question for longitudinal evidence. Economic accounts of personality also stress that behaviour depends on the task and its incentives [@almlund2011]. A trait's value cannot be inferred independently of what pupils are being asked and enabled to do.

## What the skill mix adds to previous evidence

Curiosity's prominence accords with the positive open-mindedness relationship in @avanesian2025; perseverance connects to their task-performance result. The comparison is informative at the level of skill families. Their broad domains predict high school grades, whereas our specific indices enter a joint reading pathway. Their largely parallel skill slopes across socioeconomic groups, alongside persistent differences in achievement levels, also explain why beneficial skills need not be equalising. If advantaged pupils possess more of a productive skill, similar returns to that skill can still transmit advantage.

This is close to the simple-accumulation account in @gruijters2024: socioeconomic differences in skill levels coexist with broadly similar achievement relationships across groups. Their finding of a modest explained gap tempers claims that social-emotional learning alone can close educational inequality. Our widespread positive pathways do not contradict that conclusion. The studies use different skill sets, outcomes and socioeconomic contrasts, and a count of positive pathways says little about how much of the achievement gap could be removed. Our additional question is how much the pathway changes when observed school composition is retained.

@hofer2024 likewise find mediation through self-perceptions in PISA 2018, with substantial differences across countries and measures. Their self-perceived competency pathway is stronger in more socially mobile settings, which they interpret through opportunities to use beneficial self-perceptions. Our within--between decomposition brings the role of context to the school level. Korea's prominence of enjoyment of problem solving and goal setting, alongside curiosity's broader international role, makes the institutional conditions under which particular dispositions support learning a substantive research question.

Goal setting is especially instructive. Its social gradient often coexists with a weak or negative reading contribution after other skills enter. Because the scale includes monitoring and corrective study strategies, this does not imply that ambition damages learning. It could reflect strategies adopted in response to difficulty, differences in their effective use, or overlap with other skills. Hofer et al.'s uneven findings across self-perceptions reinforce the need to explain each measure's relationship to the task [@hofer2024]. A general claim that every socially valued disposition carries advantage would miss this pattern.

## School composition as part of transmission

The school component enlarges the pathway in 27 systems. Korea and Malaysia illustrate why an individual-only account can be incomplete: family position accompanies differences in both pupils' own skills and the skill composition of the schools they attend. The inheritance-of-inequality framework recognises that families transmit access to favourable environments as well as individual characteristics [@bowles2002inheritance]. Our estimates bring these two elements into the same reading decomposition.

For an education production account, this raises a question about the allocation of inputs. Pupils may acquire similar dispositions but encounter different opportunities to use them. Alternatively, schools may contribute to the skills themselves. Jackson's evidence that teachers influence non-test-score outcomes predictive of later attainment provides an empirical reason to take the second possibility seriously [@jackson2018]. These alternatives imply different interventions: improving access to instructional opportunities, strengthening skill development within schools, or combining the two. The composition increment identifies where this distinction matters most; it does not separate these mechanisms.

Denmark supplies a useful contrast: adding the school component changes the fitted pathway relatively little. The evidence therefore supports a reproduction account whose importance depends on institutional setting. In Korea and Malaysia, evaluating pupil-level skills support together with school-level provision is particularly relevant. The observed-composition contrast is the starting point for that evaluation, not an estimate of the benefit of moving a pupil between schools. A meaningful policy comparison would measure changes in skills and reading under specific school practices, rather than assume that a favourable intake itself is an intervention.

## Material constraints and the scope of skills policy

The negative deprivation pathways in Malaysia, Mongolia and the Philippines suggest that current material constraints can enter the skills route even at similar family and school ESCS. This complements the investment mechanism in @attanasio2020, whose Colombian early-childhood experiment links developmental improvements to increased parental investments. The populations and interventions differ, but the economic implication is relevant: skill development can respond to the resources and activities surrounding children. A skills deficit need not originate in a lack of motivation.

For adolescents, unaffordable participation and restricted learning opportunities could limit exploration or sustained engagement. The coexistence of curiosity and effort-related contributions makes both plausible explanations to investigate. The less uniform deprivation evidence also matters: 25 of 63 systems show a negative joint pathway, and item sets differ across systems. These results favour country-specific examination of the constraints pupils face over a universal hardship mechanism.

The policy implication is to evaluate skills support alongside the material and instructional conditions needed to use it. Gruijters et al.'s caution about skills programmes as an inequality remedy remains pertinent [@gruijters2024]. A large mediator is not automatically the most cost-effective intervention target: programme effects, costs and reach are separate quantities. The present country results identify where the skills route, the school-composition component and deprivation warrant joint investigation. They give that investigation a more specific target than a general prescription to make disadvantaged pupils more resilient.

## Research limitations

A causal interpretation of the mediation contrast requires correct temporal ordering, adequate control of exposure--skill and skill--achievement confounding, overlap, and a sufficiently accurate model of the joint skill distribution and reading relationship. PISA measures background, skills and achievement at one occasion and does not supply prior achievement for this design. Reciprocal effects, unmeasured parental investments and school selection can therefore remain. The estimates are conditional model-based mediation contrasts; they support the proposed channels without by themselves establishing the effects of interventions on family resources, skills or school assignment. The residual-correlation stress tests in the supplement assess one form of omitted skill--outcome confounding, not all these identification conditions.

The school means capture observed composition rather than latent school traits, and are measured with error, especially in small analytic school samples [@ludtke2008]. Including these means cannot remove selection on unobserved school quality. Jointly modelled skills may influence one another; their individual contributions are an additive allocation of the joint pathway, not separately identified ordered mechanisms. Self-report response styles, measurement differences between systems and within-country standardization further limit literal comparisons of skill levels. Deprivation's coverage rule and differing item sets restrict cross-country comparability of one-item contrasts.

Complete-case analysis can change the represented population, and systems lacking the full skill block are particularly relevant to the limits of broad development claims. The main comparison is a common measured block, not a representative sample of the world's education systems. The school bootstrap incorporates clustering, re-estimation and plausible-value variation, but it is not the full PISA stratified two-stage replicate-weight procedure. Its intervals and multiple-testing counts should be read with that design limitation in mind. Finally, the specification uses additive fixed slopes: it does not test dynamic skill formation, nonlinear responses or complementarities directly. These distinctions constrain the mechanism and policy claims without changing the documented country patterns.

# Conclusion

Socio-emotional skills carry a measurable part of socioeconomic advantage in reading across much of the PISA 2025 sample. The common six-skill analysis identifies a positive joint pathway in 53 of 69 systems. Curiosity is the most widespread individual contributor, while Korea demonstrates that a strong pathway can involve a different skill composition. Material deprivation adds a distinct resource dimension, with a negative skills route in 25 of 63 systems after accounting for family and school socioeconomic status.

Including observed school composition changes the substantive interpretation. In 27 systems, the fitted skills pathway is larger with a 95% interval for the increment excluding zero. This makes it difficult to understand skill-mediated inequality solely as a difference between individual pupils. Family investments and access to learning environments belong in the same economic account.

For educational development, the priority is to identify combinations of material support, teaching practices and school conditions that expand disadvantaged pupils' opportunities to acquire and use skills. The country estimates offer a basis for choosing where to investigate those combinations. They place socio-emotional development within the production of learning inequality, while keeping the institutions and resources that shape it in view.

## Data and computation {.unnumbered}

The public-use data are available from the OECD PISA database [@oecd2026data]. The accompanying `ijed_ses_seg` research bundle contains the editable manuscript, bibliography, figure code, country tables, saved estimate snapshot and provenance checks. Rendering the draft reads those saved results and does not re-estimate the models. The supplementary PDF gives the country estimates, measurement coverage, model specifications and sensitivity results. The original estimation scripts are preserved with the bundle for inspection.
